passage:
Monday, first night of the new plan: Aparna's mother put up a paper chart: brush, pyjamas, one story, lights out at nine. Aparna argued at every step and brushed twice as slowly as usual.
Thursday, two weeks later: At ten to nine Aparna put down her crayons without being asked, went to brush, and came back holding the storybook.
Saturday, a month later, at Nani's house: There was no chart on the wall. But at nine Aparna yawned, found her toothbrush in the bag and climbed into bed with her book. Her little brother Akash was still bouncing on the mattress. "It's story time," Aparna told him, as if it were obvious.

qa.q: What four steps were on the paper chart?
qa.a: Brush, pyjamas, one story, lights out at nine.

qa.q: How can you tell Aparna felt at ease with the routine by the Saturday at Nani's?
qa.a: With no chart, she yawned at nine and went to brush on her own, calm and settled, then told Akash "It's story time" as if it were obvious.

qa.q: What choice by Aparna's mother helped the steps become automatic?
qa.a: Keeping the same order at the same time every night, so nine o'clock began the whole chain without reminders.

qa.q: How might Akash see his sister's bedtime routine?
qa.a: Akash, still bouncing, may find it strange that she stops playing on her own, but her calm lead might pull him towards the story too.

grounding: A child's bedtime steps, repeated in the same order, become automatic even in a different house.

passage: Nilesh, you ask why I still fall asleep at nine sharp? Listen. When I was eight, in our village near Ludhiana, my Bebe had a fixed way. "Sleep comes on its own, Gurleen," she used to say. After dinner we rinsed our mouths at the hand pump and rubbed our teeth with a neem twig. Then we lay on the charpais in the courtyard, and she told one story, only one, about a clever crow or a lost princess. Then the lantern went out. Every night, the same order. After a few months, Nilesh, I would start yawning the moment I tasted the neem. My feet walked to the charpai by themselves. Seventy years later, I brush, I read one page, and I'm asleep. The body remembers what you repeat.

qa.q: What did the children rub their teeth with?
qa.a: A neem twig.

qa.q: Why did young Gurleen start yawning at the taste of neem?
qa.a: After months of the same order every night, the neem had become a signal that sleep came next, so Gurleen felt calm and drowsy as the body got ready on its own.

qa.q: Which choice by Bebe made bedtime work so well?
qa.a: Keeping the same steps in the same order every night, rinse, one story, lantern out, so no step needed deciding.

qa.q: What might Nilesh take from this story?
qa.a: Nilesh may see that a steady bedtime order could make falling asleep easier, and it explains why the elder still sleeps at nine sharp.

grounding: An elder recalls how a fixed childhood bedtime order made sleep follow automatically.

passage: The wedding house in Madurai was loud until midnight, with music on the terrace and aunties laughing in every room. Kavitha, ten, was sure she would never sleep. But at half past eight she found her toothbrush in the suitcase, as she did every night at home. She brushed at the crowded sink, then went looking for her cousin Ayesha, who had promised to read to her. They squeezed onto a mattress in the storeroom, the only quiet corner, and Ayesha read one chapter by torchlight. Kavitha's eyes closed before the chapter ended. In the morning Ayesha said, "The music was so loud. How did you even sleep?" Kavitha shrugged. "It was bedtime."

qa.q: Where did Kavitha and Ayesha find a quiet corner?
qa.a: On a mattress in the storeroom.

qa.q: Why was Kavitha sure she would never sleep, and what changed?
qa.a: The house was loud with music and laughter, so sleep seemed impossible; but doing her usual steps made her body treat it as bedtime anyway.

qa.q: What choice helped Kavitha sleep despite the noise?
qa.a: Keeping her home routine, brushing at half past eight and hearing one chapter, even in a strange, crowded house.

qa.q: Why might Ayesha be surprised in the morning?
qa.a: Ayesha heard the music all night and expected a sleepless cousin, without realising how strongly the familiar steps carried Kavitha to sleep.

grounding: A child's usual bedtime steps carry her to sleep even in a noisy wedding house.

passage: At nine every night in their Mumbai flat, the pressure cooker next door gave its last whistle, and Leela, eight, put down her crayons without being asked. Brush teeth at the small basin, change into the blue pyjamas, climb into bed, wait for her mother, Seema, to open the storybook with the torn cover. One chapter, lights off. Leela didn't think about any of it anymore. The steps just rolled one into the next. One Saturday her cousin stayed over and wanted to watch TV late. Leela yawned, walked to the basin, and was halfway through brushing before she even noticed. "You're like a clock," her cousin laughed. Leela shrugged, spitting out toothpaste. "I just go."

qa.q: What sound came at nine every night?
qa.a: The pressure cooker next door gave its last whistle.

qa.q: What does 'I just go' suggest about how bedtime feels to Leela?
qa.a: Leela feels calm and at ease at bedtime; the steps are automatic rather than choices, so bedtime happens without a struggle.

qa.q: What choice could Seema make on nights when the routine is disturbed, like a cousin's visit?
qa.a: Keep the same order of steps, brushing, pyjamas and one chapter, even if the time shifts, so the familiar chain still carries Leela to sleep.

qa.q: How might the cousin see Leela's bedtime?
qa.a: The cousin, who wanted to stay up, might find it funny or puzzling that Leela leaves the TV with nobody telling her, as if a clock had ticked.

grounding: A child whose bedtime steps happen at the same time every night finds herself moving through them automatically.

"I know, Paati, I'm going." Sharmila was already at the sink with her toothbrush.

passage: Saurabh, you ask why I still fall asleep the moment my head touches the pillow? Listen. When I was a girl of nine, in our village near Nashik, my Aaji had one rule. After dinner, wash feet at the tap, brush with the neem stick, then lie on the mat for her story. Every night, same order. At first I fought it. I wanted to play marbles. But after some weeks, my feet walked to the tap on their own. Once, at my uncle's wedding, the lights and drums went on till late. Still, I washed my feet at a strange tap, brushed, and lay beside Aaji. Before her story ended, I was asleep. That is Ganga's secret, beta: the steps carry you.

qa.a: A neem stick.

qa.q: How did young Ganga feel about the bedtime rule at first, and later?
qa.a: At first she felt resistant and wanted to play marbles; later the steps felt so natural that she felt calm and fell asleep easily even at a noisy wedding.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the routine stick?
qa.a: Aaji keeping the same order every night, even on busy days, made the steps automatic for young Ganga.

qa.q: How might Aaji have felt when young Ganga fell asleep during the story at the wedding?
qa.a: Aaji may have felt pleased and tender, seeing that the routine now worked even in a noisy, unfamiliar place.

passage: The school camp at the hill station had one problem: rain. It drummed on the tents all evening, and the boys in Pranav's tent were too excited to settle. Pranav, who was nine, felt jumpy too. But at nine o'clock something odd happened. His hands found his toothbrush in the bag. At home, brushing came right before Papa's story and then lights off. So he stood under the tent flap, rinsing into the wet grass. Tenzin sir, the camp teacher, saw him. "Ready for sleep already?" Pranav nodded, surprised at himself. He lay down and asked Tenzin sir for a story. By the second page, the rain sounded far away, and his eyes were closing.

qa.q: What was drumming on the tents all evening?
qa.a: The rain was drumming on the tents.

qa.q: Why was Pranav surprised at himself when he started brushing?
qa.a: He had felt jumpy and excited, yet his hands reached for the toothbrush on their own because the routine was so familiar, which left him surprised and then calm.

qa.q: How could Tenzin sir help the other children settle?
qa.a: Tenzin sir could set a simple, repeated order each camp night, like brushing, a story and lights off, so the steps start to feel familiar.

qa.q: What is it like for Tenzin sir to see Pranav ready for sleep in all the noise?
qa.a: Tenzin sir seems pleasantly surprised and happy to help, since one calm child makes the tent easier to settle.

grounding: It shows a child whose repeated bedtime steps at home carried over automatically at a noisy, rainy camp.

passage: In their Chennai flat, Suraj had the same bedtime every night: brush teeth at half past eight, climb into bed, Amma Sunaina reads a chapter, lights out. He was ten and said he was too old for stories, but he never skipped them. Then on Wednesday Amma had to travel for work. Appa was on the phone with the office. At half past eight, Suraj looked up from his puzzle, went to the bathroom, and brushed without anyone telling him. He climbed into bed and opened the storybook himself. He read the chapter aloud, quietly, the way Amma did. Halfway through, he yawned. When Appa came in, the book was open on the blanket and Suraj was asleep.

qa.q: What time did Suraj brush his teeth every night?
qa.a: At half past eight.

qa.q: What might Suraj have felt when he went to brush without being told?
qa.a: He probably felt a little lonely without Amma but also steady and grown-up, because the familiar steps told him what came next.

qa.q: What can parents learn from Suraj's evening?
qa.a: Keeping the same order and time for bedtime steps can make them feel automatic, so a child can follow them even when routines are disrupted.

qa.q: How might Appa feel finding Suraj asleep with the book?
qa.a: Appa might feel surprised, touched and a little guilty for being on the phone, but glad the routine held on its own.

grounding: It shows a child whose bedtime steps repeated at the same time made brushing, story and sleep follow automatically, even without his mother home.

passage:
At night in our house, everything happens in the same order. First, I brush my teeth. Then Charu Didi reads me a chapter from the fat book. Then the light goes off.
It starts when the news finishes on TV, at 9. The music at the end is like a bell. I hear it and my legs walk to the bathroom before I tell them.
When we went to Nani's house in the holidays, there was no TV news, and bedtime was all mixed up. I stayed awake for ages and felt jumpy.
Now we're back. Last night, when the news music played, I was already holding my toothbrush before Didi even called me.
I like it. My body knows what to do. I don't have to think.

qa.q: What sound tells the narrator it is bedtime?
qa.a: The music at the end of the 9 o'clock TV news.

qa.q: How did the narrator feel at Nani's house when bedtime was mixed up?
qa.a: The narrator felt jumpy and stayed awake for ages without the usual order.

qa.q: Why do the narrator's bedtime steps happen “before I tell them”?
qa.a: The same cue and order every night have made the routine automatic, so no decision is needed.

qa.q: How might Charu Didi feel when she finds the narrator already holding the toothbrush?
qa.a: Charu Didi probably feels pleased and a little amused that the routine runs itself.

grounding: The child's account shows a same-time bedtime routine becoming automatic, and how it falls apart when the context changes.

House parent's note, Sunshine Children's Home, Room 4.
When Hrithik, nine, arrived in October, he wandered the corridor until eleven and woke tired and cross.
We began the same sequence nightly at 8:45: corridor bell, teeth, one story, lights out at 9:15. Same order, same time, even on weekends.
He resisted for two weeks. By week four, when the bell rang he was walking to the sink before anyone reminded him. His roommate Jomon says Hrithik “goes to brush like a robot.” Last night he fell asleep before the story ended.
The repetition seems to make the steps follow on their own.
What I did next: I shared the routine with weekend staff so it does not break when I am off.

qa.q: At what time does the bedtime bell ring?
qa.a: The corridor bell rings at 8:45.

qa.q: How did Hrithik seem to feel at bedtime when he first arrived?
qa.a: He seemed restless and cross, wandering the corridor until eleven.

qa.q: Why did the house parent share the routine with the weekend staff?
qa.a: So the same cue and order continue every night; if the context changes, the automatic steps may break.

qa.q: How does Jomon see Hrithik's new bedtime behaviour?
qa.a: Jomon finds it funny, saying Hrithik goes to brush “like a robot.”

grounding: The house parent's note shows a child's bedtime steps becoming automatic through the same cue, order and time each night.

Diwali holidays, at Nani's house
Dear diary, I am Ramesh and I am writing this in bed. Everything here is different. The house is full of cousins, the crackers go on till late, and Nani makes too many sweets.
But at nine o'clock something funny happened. Akash bhaiya said, "Brush time," and my feet just walked to the tap. I didn't even think. Then I got into the quilt and waited for a story, the same as at home. Akash bhaiya read from my old tiger book. My eyes started closing before the tiger reached the river.
At home Mummy does brush, story, sleep every night at nine. Even here, with all the noise, my body remembered.
Tomorrow is the big pooja. I hope I remember to brush without being told. I think I will.

During the Onam week, Sunaina's village in Palakkad never seemed to sleep. There were boat-race songs from the river, cousins in every room and payasam cooking late into the night.
Still, when the old clock in the hall struck nine, Sunaina put down her flower petals, went to the back verandah and picked up her toothbrush without being told. Her aunt Aparna, visiting from Chennai, watched in surprise.
"Doesn't anyone have to call you?"
Sunaina shrugged, foam on her lips. "It's nine."
After brushing, she went straight to Ammamma's room and lay down on the mat. Ammamma began the story of the clever crow, the same one she told every night. Before the crow found the pebbles, Sunaina was asleep, one hand still curled around a petal.
Aparna smiled. In the city, her own son fought bedtime every night.

qa.q: What story did Ammamma begin?
qa.a: She began the story of the clever crow.

qa.q: How did Sunaina seem to feel when the clock struck nine?
qa.a: She seemed calm and unbothered, going to brush without being told, because the routine felt natural to her.

qa.q: What might Aparna try at home after watching Sunaina?
qa.a: Aparna could set the same time each night for brushing and a story, in the same order, so her son's bedtime steps start to follow each other on their own.

qa.q: How does Aparna feel watching Sunaina fall asleep?
qa.a: Aparna seems surprised and a little wistful, thinking about how her own son fights bedtime every night in the city.

grounding: It shows a child whose steady bedtime order of brushing, a story and sleep at the same hour runs automatically even during a noisy festival week.

passage:
The long rains had come to Addis Ababa, and the power went out most evenings. Abebe's neighbour Rosa, who looked after him while his parents worked late, expected bedtime to be a battle in the dark.
But at eight, when the church bell down the road rang, Abebe got up from the floor without a word. He found the torch on the shelf, brushed his teeth at the basin by its light and climbed into bed.
"Story, Rosa," he said. "The one about the monkey and the market."
Rosa told it, rain drumming on the tin roof. Halfway through, Abebe's breathing slowed.
She sat there a while, surprised. No arguing, no "five more minutes." The bell, the brush, the story, then sleep, one step pulling the next, even with no lights at all.

qa.q: What did Abebe use to see while brushing his teeth?
qa.a: He used the torch from the shelf.

qa.q: How did Rosa feel as Abebe fell asleep?
qa.a: Rosa felt surprised and quietly pleased, because she had expected a battle and instead the routine ran smoothly.

qa.q: Why did bedtime go so smoothly even without electricity?
qa.a: Abebe's steps happen in the same order at the same time each night, starting with the eight o'clock bell, so each step follows the last without needing lights or reminders.

qa.q: What would change if Abebe's bedtime happened at different times each night?
qa.a: Without a steady cue like the bell and the same order, the steps might not follow automatically, and bedtime could turn into arguing.

grounding: It shows a child whose bedtime steps, cued by the same bell each evening, follow automatically, even during power cuts in the rainy season.

Brush teeth at the long steel sink. Pyjamas on. Everyone on their beds while Ayesha Aunty read one chapter of the story about the lost elephant. Lights out.

On the last night the generator failed and the bell never rang, but at half past eight Vaibhav was brushing his teeth by torchlight.
